title: Earth's Systems and Climate
bigQuestion: How do Earth's rock, water, air and living systems move energy and matter, and how do we know what they did in the past?

story.title: The Continents That Fit Together
story.kicker: A weather scientist noticed that South America and Africa looked like torn pieces of one page, and spent his life being told he was wrong.
paragraphs: Alfred Wegener was a German meteorologist, a weather scientist, not a geologist. Around 1910 he was looking at a world map and saw what schoolchildren still notice: the east coast of South America and the west coast of Africa look like they would fit together. Others had noticed too. Wegener did something different. He went looking for evidence, and he found a great deal of it.

The fit was better than it looked. Match the continents along the edges of their underwater shelves, not the shorelines, and the fit is tight. Rock formations in Brazil lined up with formations in West Africa. Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile, were found in both places and nowhere else; it could not have swum an ocean. A fern called Glossopteris left fossils in South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica. Scratches left by ancient glaciers in India and Africa pointed the wrong way for those continents' present positions, but made sense if they had once been joined near the South Pole.

In 1912 Wegener proposed that the continents had once formed a single landmass, which he later called Pangaea, and had slowly drifted apart. He published a book in 1915 and kept adding evidence in new editions. Most geologists rejected it, some with scorn. The problem was a fair one: Wegener could not explain what force could push continents through solid ocean floor. His guesses about the mechanism were wrong, and critics used that to dismiss the whole idea.

Wegener did not live to see the argument settled. He died in 1930 on an expedition across the Greenland ice sheet. Through the 1950s and 1960s, new tools mapped the ocean floors and measured magnetism in seafloor rock. The ocean floor was spreading apart at long mountain ridges, carrying continents with it. The continents had moved, though not the way Wegener imagined. By 1970 the idea he had been mocked for was the foundation of geology, renamed plate tectonics.
story.think: Wegener had strong evidence that continents moved but no good explanation of how. Should scientists accept a pattern before they can explain it? What would you have wanted to see?

lessons.title: Evidence From Two Shores
lessons.mainIdea: Matching coastlines, rocks, fossils and glacial scratches on separate continents are best explained by the continents once being joined.
reading: Wegener's case rested on several independent lines of evidence that all pointed the same way. That is the strongest kind of argument in science. Any one clue could have another explanation. Taken together, they fit only one story: the continents were once joined and have since moved apart.

Start with the rocks. Mountain belts in Scotland and Norway line up with the Appalachians of eastern North America when the Atlantic is closed. Ancient rock layers in Brazil match layers in West Africa in age and type. It is like tearing a newspaper and matching the lines of print across the tear. The *continental shelf*, the shallow underwater edge of each continent, gives an even tighter fit than the coastline does.

Then the fossils. Mesosaurus was a small reptile that lived in fresh water about 280 million years ago. Its bones are found in southern Africa and in Brazil and nowhere else. The seed fern Glossopteris grew across all the southern continents, and its seeds were too heavy to blow across an ocean. Before drift, geologists explained this with imaginary land bridges that had since sunk. No trace of such bridges was ever found.

Finally the climate clues. Coal, which forms in warm swamps, lies under Antarctica. Scratches carved by glaciers about 300 million years ago mark rocks in India, southern Africa, Australia and South America, places now warm. Plot them on a map with the continents rejoined around the South Pole, and the scratches all point outward from one ice cap. On today's map they make no sense at all.

words.d: Wegener's idea that the continents slowly move across Earth's surface
the shallow, gently sloping underwater edge of a continent
the single supercontinent that included all of today's continents about 250 million years ago

look.title: Wegener Makes His Case, 1915
look.text: In his book on the origin of continents and oceans, Wegener argued that the match between South America and Africa was not a coincidence, and that matching rock layers, fossils and ancient climate records on both sides of the Atlantic showed the two continents had once been joined and had drifted apart over a very long time.
look.cite: Alfred Wegener, The Origin of Continents and Oceans, 1915
look.prompt: Wegener was trained in weather, not rocks. How might that have hurt his case with geologists, and how might it have helped him see what they missed?

check.q: Why is the Mesosaurus fossil strong evidence for continental drift?
choices: It lived in fresh water, yet its fossils lie on two continents now separated by an ocean
It was the largest reptile ever found
It could swim across the Atlantic
It is found on every continent
check.why: A small freshwater reptile could not cross salt ocean. Finding it only in Brazil and southern Africa fits those lands once touching.

check.q: Ancient glacial scratches in India point in a direction that makes no sense today. What explains them?
choices: India used to be much colder because the sun was dimmer
India was once joined with other southern lands near the South Pole
The scratches were made by rivers, not ice
Earth's poles used to be near the equator
check.why: Rejoining the southern continents around the pole makes the scratches radiate out from one ice cap, as glaciers actually flow.

check.q: Why does using several independent lines of evidence make a scientific case stronger?
choices: More evidence is always right
It takes longer to collect
Each clue could have another explanation, but all of them together fit only one story
Scientists vote on the total
check.why: One clue can be a coincidence. When rocks, fossils and climate all independently point the same way, coincidence becomes very unlikely.

lessons.title: The Ocean Floor Speaks
lessons.mainIdea: New crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outward, recorded in magnetic stripes and in seafloor that gets older away from the ridge.
reading: For most of history no one knew what the ocean floor looked like. During and after World War II, ships with echo sounders traced its shape. Instead of a flat plain, they found a mountain chain running down the middle of the Atlantic and around the globe, 65,000 kilometers long, with a deep crack along its crest. This was the *mid-ocean ridge*. It was volcanic, hot, and shaken by small earthquakes.

In 1962 Harry Hess proposed *seafloor spreading*: molten rock rises at the ridge, hardens into new ocean crust, and the two sides move apart. Old crust sinks back into Earth at deep ocean trenches. A test came fast. Earth's magnetic field flips direction every few hundred thousand years, and lava locks in the field's direction as it cools. If Hess was right, the seafloor should carry stripes of normal and reversed magnetism, mirrored on both sides of the ridge.

In 1963 Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews published exactly that pattern from ship surveys. The stripes were symmetric, like a tape recording played from the center out. Later, drill cores showed that seafloor rock gets older the farther it lies from the ridge. The oldest ocean floor anywhere is only about 180 million years old, while continents hold rocks 4 billion years old. Ocean floor is constantly made and destroyed.

Today the spreading is measured directly. Satellite positioning tracks stations on different continents and shows them moving a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. The Atlantic widens by roughly 2.5 centimeters each year. Wegener's continents do move, but they ride on plates of crust and upper mantle, and the ocean floor moves with them.

words.d: an underwater mountain chain where new ocean crust forms as plates move apart
the formation of new ocean floor at a ridge, pushing older floor away on both sides
a flip in the direction of Earth's magnetic field, which happens every few hundred thousand years

look.title: A Tape Recorder Made of Rock
look.text: A ship tows a magnetometer back and forth across the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The instrument records a stripe of rock magnetized in today's direction along the ridge crest, then a stripe magnetized backward, then normal again, then reversed. On the far side of the ridge, the same sequence appears in mirror image.
look.prompt: Why does a mirrored pattern on both sides of the ridge support the idea that new crust forms at the crest and moves outward in both directions?

check.q: Where is the youngest ocean crust found?
choices: Near the continents
At the deep ocean trenches
At the crest of the mid-ocean ridge
In the middle of the Pacific
check.why: New crust forms at the ridge and moves away. Rock gets older with distance from the ridge crest.

check.q: Why is no ocean floor older than about 180 million years?
choices: Oceans did not exist before then
The seafloor is too deep to sample
Older ocean rocks dissolve in seawater
Old ocean crust is recycled back into Earth at trenches
check.why: Ocean crust is made at ridges and destroyed at trenches. Continents are lighter and stay at the surface, so they keep far older rocks.

check.q: What made the magnetic stripe pattern a good test of seafloor spreading?
choices: The prediction was specific: mirrored stripes on both sides of the ridge
Magnets are easy to find
The stripes are visible from space
The stripes are all the same width
check.why: Hess's idea predicted a symmetric pattern that no other idea did. Finding it in 1963 was a strong confirmation.

lessons.title: Where Plates Meet
lessons.mainIdea: Earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains cluster along plate boundaries where plates spread apart, collide or slide past each other.
reading: Earth's outer shell is broken into about a dozen large *tectonic plates* and several small ones, each moving a few centimeters a year. Plot the world's earthquakes on a map and they trace the plate edges in sharp lines. Volcanoes do too. The action is at the boundaries, and there are three kinds.

At a *divergent boundary* plates pull apart. Magma rises to fill the gap and hardens into new crust. The mid-ocean ridges are the main example, and Iceland sits right on one, which is why it has so many volcanoes. On land, East Africa is slowly splitting along a rift valley. At a *convergent boundary* plates push together. When ocean crust meets a continent, the denser ocean plate dives beneath in a process called subduction, melting and feeding volcanoes like those of the Cascades and the Andes. When two continents collide, neither sinks, and the crust crumples upward into mountains. The Himalayas are India still ramming into Asia.

At a *transform boundary* plates slide past each other sideways. The San Andreas Fault in California is one. Rock on either side snags, strain builds for decades, then the fault slips in seconds. That sudden slip is an earthquake. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake moved the ground along the fault by several meters.

Illinois sits deep inside the North American plate, far from any edge, so big quakes are rare here. Not impossible, though. The New Madrid seismic zone in the Mississippi Valley near southern Illinois produced a series of powerful earthquakes in 1811 and 1812 that rang church bells hundreds of miles away. Geologists think an ancient, failed rift, a weak spot from long ago, is being squeezed by today's plate motions. Small quakes still happen in southern Illinois every year.

words.d: one of the large rigid pieces of Earth's outer shell that move slowly over the mantle
a place where two plates move apart and new crust forms
a place where two plates push together, causing subduction or mountain building
a place where two plates slide past each other sideways
the sinking of a denser plate beneath another plate into the mantle

look.title: The Earthquake Map
look.text: A world map is dotted with every earthquake stronger than magnitude 5 from the past twenty years. The dots are not scattered evenly. They form narrow belts: one rings the whole Pacific Ocean, one snakes down the middle of the Atlantic, one runs from the Mediterranean through the Himalayas. Vast areas, including most of Illinois, are nearly blank.
look.prompt: What do the belts mark, and why does the ring around the Pacific hold both the most earthquakes and the most volcanoes?

check.q: Which type of boundary creates new crust?
choices: Transform
Convergent between two continents
Subduction zone
Divergent
check.why: At a divergent boundary plates pull apart and magma fills the gap, forming new crust as at the mid-ocean ridges.

check.q: Why do the Himalayas keep growing?
choices: Two continental plates are colliding and neither can sink
Ocean crust is subducting under Asia
The plates there are sliding sideways
Volcanoes are piling up lava
check.why: Continental crust is too light to subduct. When India pushes into Asia the crust thickens and folds upward.

check.q: Why are large earthquakes rare in Illinois?
choices: Illinois is on a divergent boundary
Illinois lies far inside a plate, not at a boundary
The soil in Illinois absorbs shaking
Illinois has no faults at all
check.why: Most quakes happen at plate edges. Illinois is deep inside the North American plate, though the New Madrid zone shows that interior quakes can occur.

lessons.title: Layers Seen by Earthquake Waves
lessons.mainIdea: Seismic waves bending and stopping inside Earth reveal a solid crust and mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.
reading: The deepest hole ever drilled reaches about 12 kilometers. Earth's center is 6,371 kilometers down. Nobody has seen the inside, yet we know its layers with confidence. The evidence comes from earthquakes. Each big quake sends *seismic waves* through the whole planet, and instruments called seismographs on every continent record when they arrive. From the timing, scientists work out what the waves passed through.

Two kinds of waves matter most. P waves are push-pull waves like sound and travel through solids and liquids. S waves shake sideways and travel only through solids; a liquid cannot carry a sideways shake. In 1906 Richard Oldham noticed that S waves never arrived on the side of Earth opposite a quake. Something in the middle stopped them. In 1914 Beno Gutenberg pinned down its edge: a liquid core beginning about 2,900 kilometers down.

In 1936 the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann studied faint P waves arriving where they should not have. She showed that inside the liquid outer *core* sits a solid inner core. Above the core is the *mantle*, about 2,900 kilometers of hot, dense rock. It is solid but can flow very slowly, like extremely stiff putty. On top is the thin *crust*. It is about 5 to 10 kilometers thick under oceans and around 35 kilometers under continents, thicker under mountains.

Other evidence backs up the picture. Earth's overall density, about 5.5 times that of water, is much higher than surface rock, so the inside must be heavy: iron and nickel fit. Iron meteorites, the broken cores of shattered small planets, show what such a core would be like. And the swirling of liquid iron in the outer core generates Earth's magnetic field, which is why the compass works and why the seafloor could record the field's reversals.

words.d: a vibration that travels through Earth from an earthquake or explosion
Earth's thin, rocky outer layer, thinner under oceans than under continents
the thick layer of hot, slowly flowing solid rock between the crust and the core
Earth's iron-rich center, liquid on the outside and solid at the very middle

look.title: How Deep the Layers Go
rows: Base of the liquid outer core
look.prompt: About what fraction of the distance to Earth's center is the crust? Why did people once think the crust was a much bigger part of the planet?

check.q: How did scientists learn that Earth's outer core is liquid?
choices: They drilled into it
S waves, which cannot pass through liquid, do not reach the far side of Earth
Lava from volcanoes comes from the core
The core is too hot to be measured
check.why: S waves shake sideways and need a solid to travel. Their shadow on the opposite side of Earth revealed a liquid layer in the middle.

check.q: What did Inge Lehmann discover in 1936?
choices: The mantle is liquid
Earth's crust is thicker under oceans
A solid inner core inside the liquid outer core
Earthquakes happen only at plate edges
check.why: She traced faint P waves that had reflected off a boundary inside the core and showed a solid center exists.

check.q: Why must Earth's interior be made of something denser than surface rock?
choices: Because volcanoes erupt heavy lava
Because the mantle flows
Because compasses point north
Because the planet's overall density is far higher than the rock at the surface
check.why: Earth averages about 5.5 times the density of water, but crustal rock is only about 3. Heavy iron deep inside makes up the difference.

lessons.title: Heat Moving Rock
lessons.mainIdea: Heat from Earth's formation and from radioactive decay drives slow convection in the mantle, and that motion moves the plates.
reading: Wegener's critics asked the right question: what could possibly move a continent? The answer is heat. Earth's interior is hot for two reasons. Some heat is left over from the planet's violent birth, when colliding rock and sinking iron released huge energy. The rest comes from *radioactive decay* of uranium, thorium and potassium in the mantle and crust, which produces heat steadily and will for billions of years.

Heat inside must find a way out. In the mantle it does so by *convection*. Hot rock deep down is slightly less dense, so it rises very slowly; cooler rock near the top is denser and sinks. The same thing happens in a pot of thick soup on a stove, only the mantle moves centimeters per year instead of centimeters per second. Mantle rock is solid, but over millions of years it flows.

The plates ride on top of this and take part in it. At ridges, hot mantle wells up and new plate forms. As plate moves away from the ridge it cools, thickens and grows denser. Eventually its edge is dense enough to sink at a trench. The sinking slab pulls the rest of the plate behind it, a force geologists call *slab pull*, now thought to be the biggest single push on plate motion. Wegener was not wrong that continents move; he was wrong about why, and the why took another fifty years.

You can see the heat escaping. Volcanoes, hot springs and geysers at Yellowstone are mantle heat reaching the surface. The temperature in deep mines rises about 25 degrees Celsius for every kilometer down. Geothermal power plants in Iceland and California tap this heat directly, and heat pumps in Illinois homes use the steady temperature just a few meters underground.

words.d: the movement of heat by hot material rising and cool material sinking
the breakdown of unstable atoms, which releases heat inside Earth
the force of a cold, dense plate edge sinking into the mantle and dragging its plate along

look.title: Soup on the Stove
look.text: A pot of thick tomato soup heats on a burner. At first it is still. Then a slow bulge rises in the middle, spreads across the top, cools, and slides down along the edges of the pot. A few crackers floating on the surface drift outward from the rising center, bump into each other at the edges, and one gets dragged under.
look.prompt: Which parts of this scene stand for the mantle, the mid-ocean ridge, the plates and a subduction trench?

check.q: What are the two main sources of Earth's internal heat?
choices: Sunlight and tides
Heat left from Earth's formation and radioactive decay
Volcanoes and earthquakes
Ocean currents and wind
check.why: Leftover heat from the planet's assembly plus steady heat from decaying uranium, thorium and potassium keep the interior hot.

check.q: In mantle convection, why does hot rock rise?
choices: It is pushed up by the core
It is lighter because it contains more gas
It is slightly less dense than the cooler rock around it
Gravity is weaker deep in the mantle
check.why: Heating makes rock expand slightly and become less dense. Less dense material rises, just as in a heated pot of soup.

check.q: What is now thought to be the largest force moving plates?
choices: Earth's rotation
The moon's pull
Wind on the continents
A cold, dense plate edge sinking and pulling its plate along
check.why: Slab pull, the weight of subducting plate, drags the rest of the plate toward the trench and outpaces other forces.

lessons.title: The Rock Cycle at Scale
lessons.mainIdea: Plate motion, heat, water and time move rock through igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic forms over and over.
reading: Pick up a chunk of limestone from a quarry near Chicago and you are holding an old sea floor. Illinois was under a warm, shallow ocean about 300 to 450 million years ago. Shells and coral skeletons piled up, were buried and pressed, and became stone. The state's coal formed later, from swamp forests buried in mud. Rocks are not permanent. They are stages in a cycle powered by heat inside Earth and by the sun and water outside it.

The cycle has three families. *Igneous rock* forms when melted rock cools, either underground into granite or on the surface into basalt and volcanic ash. *Sedimentary rock* forms when broken pieces, or minerals from water, settle in layers and cement together: sandstone, shale, limestone. *Metamorphic rock* forms when heat and pressure change an existing rock without melting it: limestone into marble, shale into slate.

Plate tectonics runs the deep parts of the cycle. Subduction carries sediment and ocean crust down to melt and return as volcanic rock. Colliding plates squeeze rock into mountains and cook it into metamorphic forms. Then the sun-driven part takes over. Rain, ice and wind break mountains into grains, rivers carry the grains to the sea, and layers build up again. Over hundreds of millions of years the same atoms may pass through all three families several times.

The record is not neat. A rock layer can be missing because it eroded before the next formed, and a gap in the layers is a gap in time. Even so, layers have an order, oldest at the bottom unless something has overturned them. Combine that order with radioactive dates from volcanic ash and you get a calendar of Earth's history. Illinois's own rocks, read this way, tell of seas, deltas, swamps and finally glaciers.

words.d: rock formed when melted rock cools and hardens
rock formed from layers of settled particles or minerals that cement together
rock changed by heat and pressure without melting
the wearing away and carrying off of rock and soil by water, ice and wind

look.title: The Quarry Wall
look.text: A limestone quarry wall south of Chicago shows dozens of flat gray layers stacked like pages. In one layer you can pick out fossil shells and a piece of coral. Above the limestone lies dark shale, then a thin black seam of coal, then loose gravel and sand with rounded pebbles of granite, a rock that does not form anywhere in Illinois.
look.prompt: Read the wall from bottom to top. What sequence of environments does it record, and where might the granite pebbles have come from?

check.q: Limestone under Chicago is evidence that Illinois once:
choices: Was covered by a shallow sea
Had active volcanoes
Was at the South Pole
Had no life
check.why: Limestone forms from shells and coral skeletons piling up on a sea floor. Fossils in it confirm the marine setting.

check.q: Shale is buried deep and squeezed by colliding plates until it becomes slate. What kind of change is this?
choices: Igneous
Metamorphic
Sedimentary
Erosion
check.why: Heat and pressure changed the rock without melting it. That is the definition of metamorphic change.

check.q: What powers the surface half of the rock cycle, breaking mountains into sediment?
choices: Radioactive decay in the core
Subduction
The sun and water, through weather, rivers and ice
Earth's magnetic field
check.why: Rain, ice, wind and rivers, all driven by solar energy and gravity, wear down rock and carry the pieces to new places.

lessons.title: Water on the Move
lessons.mainIdea: Solar energy lifts water from the oceans and gravity brings it back, moving heat and shaping land as it goes.
reading: Almost all of Earth's water, about 97 percent, is salty ocean. Of the fresh water that remains, most is locked in ice sheets and glaciers or stored underground. Lakes and rivers, the water we can see, are a tiny sliver. Yet the water cycle moves an enormous amount. The sun *evaporates* water from the oceans, winds carry the vapor, and it falls as rain and snow, some of it on land, where it runs back to the sea or soaks into the ground.

Water is a heat carrier. Turning liquid water into vapor takes a lot of energy, and that energy is released again when the vapor *condenses* into cloud droplets. Warm tropical oceans load the air with vapor; when it condenses far away, it warms the air there. Much of the heat that moves from the equator toward the poles travels this way, as water vapor in the air and as warm currents in the sea. The Gulf Stream keeps northern Europe far milder than its latitude would suggest.

Water also works on rock. Rain slightly acidic with dissolved carbon dioxide slowly dissolves limestone, carving caves and sinkholes. Rivers carry sediment: the Mississippi hauls millions of tons of Illinois and Midwestern soil to the Gulf of Mexico every year, building the delta. Ice does more. Glaciers gouged the Great Lakes basins and left the flat, fertile plains of Illinois. Where water goes, the land changes.

Illinois sits beside one of the largest stores of fresh surface water on Earth. The five Great Lakes together hold about a fifth of the world's liquid fresh surface water. Chicago drinks from Lake Michigan and, since 1900, sends its treated wastewater away from the lake by a reversed river. That *watershed* decision, where each drop ends up, shapes politics, farming and city life across the whole region.

words.d: to change from liquid to vapor, which takes in energy
to change from vapor to liquid, which gives off energy
the whole area of land that drains to one river, lake or sea
loose particles of rock, soil or shell carried and deposited by water, wind or ice

look.title: The Great Lakes by Surface Area
look.prompt: Lake Michigan is the only Great Lake entirely inside the United States. Roughly what fraction of the five lakes' total surface does it hold?

check.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water?
choices: In rivers
In the atmosphere
In lakes
In ice sheets, glaciers and underground
check.why: Rivers and lakes are a tiny share. Most fresh water is frozen at the poles or stored as groundwater.

check.q: How does water vapor carry heat from the tropics toward the poles?
choices: Evaporation takes in energy in warm places, and condensation releases it far away
Vapor is hotter than liquid water
Clouds reflect heat toward the poles
Rain is warmer than the ocean
check.why: Energy absorbed when water evaporates is hidden in the vapor and released wherever it condenses, warming that air.

check.q: What carved the basins of the Great Lakes?
choices: Earthquakes along a rift
Glaciers during the ice age
The Mississippi River
Volcanic collapse
check.why: Ice sheets gouged and deepened river valleys, and meltwater filled the basins as the ice retreated.

lessons.title: Carbon and the Blanket of Air
lessons.mainIdea: Carbon cycles among air, water, rock and life; the carbon dioxide in the air traps heat and keeps Earth warm enough for liquid water.
reading: Earth without its atmosphere would average about 18 degrees Celsius below freezing. The actual average is about 15 degrees above. The difference comes from a few gases that let sunlight in but slow the escape of heat. This is the *greenhouse effect*, and it is why the planet has liquid oceans. Water vapor is the largest part of it. *Carbon dioxide* and methane do the rest, and unlike water vapor they linger long enough to set the overall temperature.

The physics was measured, not guessed. In 1859 John Tyndall in London passed heat radiation through tubes of different gases. Nitrogen and oxygen let it through. Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapor absorbed it strongly. In 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated by hand how much warmer Earth would get if the carbon dioxide in the air doubled. His answer was a few degrees, in the same range as modern estimates.

Carbon does not stay put. Plants pull carbon dioxide from the air to build leaves and wood; animals and decay return it. The oceans dissolve it and shells lock it into limestone. Volcanoes leak it back out over millions of years. This *carbon cycle* stayed roughly balanced for a long time, with carbon dioxide near 280 parts per million for thousands of years before the 1800s.

Fossil fuels are carbon that was buried for hundreds of millions of years. Burning coal, oil and gas returns it to the air in a few centuries. Direct measurements at Mauna Loa in Hawaii, begun in 1958, show carbon dioxide rising every year, past 420 parts per million by the early 2020s. The added carbon carries the chemical fingerprint of ancient plants, not volcanoes. The ocean, absorbing part of it, has become measurably more acidic. These are measurements, checked by many groups, not projections.

words.d: the warming of a planet by gases that let sunlight in but slow the escape of heat
a gas of one carbon and two oxygen atoms, released by breathing, decay, volcanoes and burning
the movement of carbon among air, oceans, rock and living things
a way to state a small concentration; 400 ppm means 400 molecules out of every million

look.title: Carbon Dioxide in the Air at Mauna Loa
look.prompt: By how much did the number rise in each 20-year span? Is the rise steady, slowing, or speeding up?

check.q: What did Tyndall's 1859 experiment show?
choices: Nitrogen absorbs heat radiation strongly
The air has no effect on heat
Carbon dioxide and water vapor absorb heat radiation while nitrogen and oxygen do not
Earth is cooling
check.why: Tyndall measured which gases block heat radiation. The greenhouse gases did; the main gases of the air did not.

check.q: How do scientists know the added carbon dioxide comes from fossil fuels rather than volcanoes?
choices: Volcanoes stopped erupting in 1958
There is no way to tell
The ocean has become less acidic
The added carbon has the chemical fingerprint of ancient plants
check.why: Carbon from buried plants has a distinct isotope signature. The air's carbon has shifted toward that signature as fossil fuel use grew.

check.q: Without any greenhouse gases, Earth's average temperature would be:
choices: Well below freezing
About the same as now
Hotter than now
Exactly zero degrees
check.why: Sunlight alone would leave Earth averaging about minus 18 degrees Celsius. Greenhouse gases raise it to about plus 15.

lessons.title: Feedbacks Between Systems
lessons.mainIdea: Earth's systems push back on each other; some feedbacks amplify a change and some dampen it.
reading: Earth's air, water, ice, rock and life are not separate. Change one and the others respond, and their response can make the first change bigger or smaller. Scientists call such a loop a *feedback*. A microphone too near its speaker squeals: sound goes in, comes out louder, goes back in. That is a *positive feedback*, which amplifies. A thermostat that shuts off the furnace when the room warms is a *negative feedback*, which stabilizes.

Ice gives a clear positive feedback. Snow and sea ice are bright and reflect most sunlight back to space. Open water and bare ground are dark and absorb it. If warming melts some ice, more sunlight is absorbed, which warms things more, which melts more ice. The Arctic has warmed faster than the rest of the planet partly for this reason. The loop runs the other way too: growing ice cools, which grows more ice, one reason ice ages deepened once they began.

Water vapor is another amplifier. Warmer air holds more vapor, and vapor is itself a greenhouse gas, so a warming from any cause gets roughly doubled. On the dampening side, warmer air radiates more heat to space, which limits how far a warming can go. Over very long times, rock weathering acts as a thermostat: warmer, wetter climates dissolve rock faster, which pulls carbon dioxide out of the air and cools things back down. That takes hundreds of thousands of years, too slow to help on human timescales.

Life is in the loop as well. Forests take up carbon and release moisture that makes clouds. Ocean plankton produce gases that seed clouds. Thawing permafrost releases carbon that was frozen for thousands of years. Untangling which feedbacks dominate, and how fast, is a major part of climate science, and it is where much of the honest uncertainty in projections comes from.

words.d: a loop in which the result of a change acts back on the cause
a loop that makes a change bigger, such as melting ice absorbing more sunlight
a loop that pushes back against a change and steadies the system
the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects; snow is high, open ocean is low

look.title: Two Parking Lots in July
look.text: Two parking lots sit side by side on a July afternoon in Chicago. One is fresh black asphalt. The other has been painted white. You walk barefoot across both. The black lot burns your feet; the white one is merely warm. That night the black lot still radiates heat you can feel from a meter away.
look.prompt: Apply this to an ocean that loses its summer sea ice. What changes about the energy it takes in, and why does that change feed on itself?

check.q: Which is an example of a positive feedback?
choices: A thermostat turning off a furnace
Melting ice exposing dark water that absorbs more sunlight
Warmer air radiating more heat to space
Rock weathering removing carbon dioxide
check.why: Melting leads to more absorbed sunlight, which leads to more melting. The loop amplifies the original change.

check.q: Why does rock weathering not prevent warming on human timescales?
choices: It only works when the climate is cold
It adds carbon dioxide instead of removing it
It takes hundreds of thousands of years to act
It stopped when the ice ages ended
check.why: Weathering is a real negative feedback, but it is far too slow to offset changes that take decades.

check.q: Warmer air holds more water vapor, and water vapor traps heat. What kind of feedback is this?
choices: A stabilizing feedback
No feedback at all
A feedback that cools the planet
A positive feedback that amplifies warming
check.why: The result of warming, more vapor, causes more warming. That is amplification, a positive feedback.

lessons.title: Bubbles in Ancient Ice
lessons.mainIdea: Ice cores hold layers of old snow and trapped air that record temperature and carbon dioxide for hundreds of thousands of years.
reading: Snow that falls on Antarctica or Greenland does not melt. It piles up, year on year, and presses into ice. Each year's layer traps tiny bubbles of that year's air. Drill straight down and you pull up a column of frozen time. The deepest *ice cores* from Antarctica reach back about 800,000 years. Reading them is like reading tree rings, if each ring also held a sealed sample of the sky.

The bubbles give carbon dioxide and methane directly, by cracking the ice in a vacuum and measuring the gas. Temperature comes from the ice itself. Water molecules come in slightly heavier and lighter forms, and colder air leaves snow with fewer of the heavy ones. The ratio of heavy to light water in each layer is a *proxy* for the temperature when it fell. Dust in the layers records droughts and wind; ash records volcanoes; sulfur spikes match known eruptions and help check the dates.

The cores show a rhythm. Over the past 800,000 years, ice ages and warm periods have alternated on roughly 100,000-year cycles, paced by slow wobbles in Earth's orbit and tilt. Through all those cycles, carbon dioxide swung between about 180 parts per million in the coldest times and about 280 in the warmest. Temperature and carbon dioxide rise and fall together. Today's level, above 420, is higher than anything in the entire record.

Ice is not the only archive. Ocean sediment cores, cave formations, coral bands, tree rings and lake mud each record different times and places. They are dated by counting layers and by radioactive decay, and where they overlap they agree. Any single record could be misread. It is the agreement among independent archives that gives confidence about past climate.

words.d: a long cylinder of ice drilled from an ice sheet, holding layers of ancient snow and air
something measured in place of what you really want to know, such as heavy water as a stand-in for temperature
a long cold period when ice sheets spread over large parts of the continents

look.title: A Meter of Deep Ice
look.text: On a lab table lies a meter-long cylinder of ice from 3 kilometers deep in Antarctica, cloudy with tiny bubbles. A thin dark band crosses it partway along. When a piece is melted in a sealed chamber, the released gas measures 190 parts per million carbon dioxide, and the water is rich in the lighter kind of water molecule.
look.prompt: What was the climate like when this snow fell, what might the dark band be, and how could you check the layer's age against something outside the core?

check.q: How do ice cores reveal the carbon dioxide of the past?
choices: Air bubbles trapped in each year's snow hold samples of that year's air
Carbon dioxide turns ice blue
Scientists measure how fast the ice melts
The ice absorbs gas from the air today
check.why: Snow traps air as it packs into ice. Cracking the ice in a vacuum releases the original air for measurement.

check.q: What does the ratio of heavy to light water in ice tell scientists?
choices: How much snow fell
The temperature when the snow fell
How deep the ice is
How salty the ocean was
check.why: Colder air leaves fewer heavy water molecules in snow, so the ratio serves as a temperature proxy.

check.q: How does today's carbon dioxide compare with the 800,000-year ice core record?
choices: It is about average
It matches the coldest ice ages
It is higher than anything in the record
It is lower than any warm period
check.why: The record swings between about 180 and 280 parts per million. Today's level is above 420, far outside that range.

lessons.title: Models and Projections
lessons.mainIdea: Climate models apply the laws of physics to the whole planet, are tested against the past, and give ranges rather than exact forecasts.
reading: A *climate model* is not a crystal ball. It is a large computer program that divides the atmosphere and ocean into millions of boxes and applies the same physics used for weather: how air moves, how water evaporates and condenses, how sunlight and heat radiation pass through gases. The first simple versions in the 1960s could be run on paper. Today's versions run on supercomputers and include ice, vegetation and the carbon cycle.

The models are tested before they are trusted. Run one from 1900 with the known changes in sunlight, volcanoes and greenhouse gases and it should reproduce the warming that thermometers actually recorded. It does, and it fails to if greenhouse gases are left out. Models predicted in the 1980s that the lower atmosphere would warm while the upper atmosphere cooled, that nights would warm faster than days, and that the Arctic would warm fastest. All three later showed up in measurements.

A *projection* is not a *prediction*. Models cannot know how much fuel people will burn in 2050, so scientists run them under several scenarios, from rapid cuts to continued growth. Each scenario gives a range, because the feedbacks, especially clouds, are not pinned down. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reviews thousands of studies. Its reports say Earth has already warmed about 1.1 degrees Celsius since the late 1800s. How much further it warms depends mostly on future emissions.

Honest science states its limits. Regional details, the timing of ice sheet changes, and the exact strength of cloud feedback carry real uncertainty. What is not uncertain is the direction: more greenhouse gas means a warmer planet, from physics measured in 1859. Models sharpen the picture; they did not create it. Students in Illinois can test the reasoning themselves by looking at how the state's own growing season, frost dates and heavy rains have shifted over the past century.

words.d: a computer program that applies physical laws to simulate the atmosphere, oceans, ice and land
what a model shows would happen under a stated set of assumptions, such as a level of future emissions
a definite statement of what will happen; models give ranges, not single predictions
one possible future path of emissions or other choices used as input to a model

look.title: Arrhenius Estimates a Doubling, 1896
look.text: In a paper on the effect of carbonic acid in the air on ground temperature, the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius worked out by hand, using measurements of how the air absorbs heat, that doubling the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere would raise Earth's surface temperature by several degrees, with a larger effect near the poles than at the equator.
look.prompt: Arrhenius had no computer and worked from a few gas measurements. Which parts of his conclusion have held up, and what might a modern model add that he could not?

check.q: How is a climate model tested?
choices: By asking experts whether they like the results
By checking that it is the most complex program available
By running it from the past and comparing its output to what thermometers actually recorded
By adjusting it until it shows warming
check.why: A model that reproduces the measured history of the past century, and fails without greenhouse gases, has earned some trust.

check.q: Why do models give a range of future temperatures rather than one number?
choices: Because computers are too slow
Because scientists disagree about whether the greenhouse effect is real
Because Earth's past climate is unknown
Because future emissions and some feedbacks, especially clouds, are uncertain
check.why: The inputs depend on human choices, and cloud feedback strength is not pinned down, so results are reported as ranges under scenarios.

check.q: Which prediction made in the 1980s was later confirmed by measurements?
choices: Nights warming faster than days
The poles cooling
The oceans getting less acidic
Carbon dioxide falling
check.why: Models predicted faster night warming, upper-atmosphere cooling and fast Arctic warming, and all three were later observed.

lessons.title: How the Great Lakes Were Made
lessons.mainIdea: Ice sheets a kilometer thick scraped out the Great Lakes basins and flattened Illinois, then melted back about 14,000 years ago.
reading: Stand on the lakefront in Chicago and look north across water that stretches to the horizon. Lake Michigan is about 500 kilometers long and in places 280 meters deep. No river could dig that. The lakes are the work of ice. During the last *ice age*, the Laurentide ice sheet spread from Canada across the northern United States. At its greatest extent, about 20,000 years ago, ice more than a kilometer thick covered most of Illinois.

A glacier is a slow bulldozer. Its weight and motion pluck rock from the ground and drag it along. The ice sheet followed old river valleys in soft rock and gouged them deeper and wider into the basins of the Great Lakes. When it reached harder rock, it scraped and polished it. The ground-up rock, from boulders to flour-fine clay, was carried south and dumped in a blanket geologists call *glacial till*. The flat, deep, fertile soil of central Illinois is mostly this till, topped by windblown dust from the dried-out glacial floodplains.

The ice began to melt back about 18,000 years ago. Where its edge paused, it left ridges of rubble called *moraines*; the low hills that curve around Chicago's suburbs are moraines. Meltwater filled the basins in front of the retreating ice. An early, larger version of Lake Michigan, which geologists call Lake Chicago, stood higher than today's lake and drained south through the Illinois River valley. Its old shorelines still show up as low ridges in the city. By about 14,000 years ago most of Illinois was ice-free, and the lakes have settled into their present shapes over the thousands of years since.

The evidence is everywhere once you know to look. Granite boulders lie in Illinois fields, hundreds of kilometers from any granite bedrock, carried down from Canada. Grooves scratched by rock in the ice mark exposed bedrock. Layers of till stack up from more than one glacial advance. The Great Lakes are young by Earth's standards, a few thousand years old in their current form, and still slowly changing as the land, freed of the ice's weight, rises a few millimeters a year.

words.d: a long cold period when ice sheets cover large parts of the continents
the unsorted mix of clay, sand, gravel and boulders dropped by a melting glacier
a ridge of rock and soil piled up at the edge of a glacier
a glacier large enough to cover a whole region or continent

look.title: A Geologist Reads the Boulders
look.text: In his 1840 book on glaciers, the Swiss scientist Louis Agassiz argued that the scattered boulders, polished bedrock and scratched surfaces found far from any mountains across northern Europe could not have been left by floods, and were instead the marks of vast sheets of ice that had once covered the land and later melted away.
look.cite: Louis Agassiz, Études sur les glaciers (Studies on Glaciers), 1840
look.prompt: Before Agassiz, many people explained scattered boulders with a great flood. What could a glacier do that a flood could not, and how would the evidence differ?

check.q: Where did the granite boulders in Illinois farm fields come from?
choices: Ancient Illinois volcanoes
Carried from Canada by the ice sheet
Deposited by the Mississippi River
Meteorites
check.why: Illinois has no granite bedrock. The boulders were plucked from the Canadian Shield and dragged south by the glacier.

check.q: What are the low hills curving around Chicago's suburbs?
choices: Old sand dunes
Folded rock from a plate collision
Moraines left where the ice edge paused
Piles of river sediment
check.why: As the ice sheet melted back, it dropped rubble at each pause in its retreat, forming curved ridges called moraines.

check.q: Why is central Illinois so flat and fertile?
choices: It was never touched by glaciers
It was the bottom of the ocean until recently
Volcanic ash built up its soil
Glaciers spread a thick blanket of ground-up rock over the old landscape
check.why: Glacial till and windblown dust buried the older hills and valleys under deep, mineral-rich soil.

review.q: What problem kept most geologists from accepting Wegener's idea in the 1920s?
choices: He could not explain what force moved the continents
The continents do not actually fit together
No fossils matched across the Atlantic
He had never seen a map
review.why: Wegener's evidence was strong, but his proposed mechanisms were wrong, and critics used that to reject the whole idea.

review.q: Which discovery in the 1960s confirmed that ocean floor spreads from the ridges?
choices: Coal under Antarctica
Mirrored magnetic stripes on both sides of the mid-ocean ridge
The New Madrid earthquakes
Glacial scratches in India
review.why: Vine and Matthews found symmetric stripes recording magnetic reversals, exactly as seafloor spreading predicted.

review.q: Which observation shows Earth's outer core is liquid?
choices: Lava is liquid
The crust floats
S waves do not pass through it
The core is hot
review.why: S waves need a solid. Their shadow zone on the far side of Earth revealed a liquid layer.

review.q: What drives the slow motion of the mantle?
choices: Ocean tides
The sun's heat
Wind
Heat from Earth's formation and radioactive decay causing convection
review.why: Internal heat makes deep rock rise and cool rock sink, a convection that carries the plates.

review.q: A cave forms as slightly acidic rainwater dissolves rock. Which rock is it most likely dissolving?
choices: Limestone
Granite
Basalt
Slate
review.why: Limestone, made of calcium carbonate, dissolves in weak acid. Illinois and Kentucky caves are cut in it.

review.q: Why do ice cores show carbon dioxide and temperature rising and falling together over the past 800,000 years?
choices: Because scientists adjusted the data
Because carbon dioxide traps heat and warming releases more carbon dioxide from the oceans, a feedback
Because ice cores cannot measure gases
Because volcanoes erupt more in warm periods
review.why: Orbital cycles start the change; carbon dioxide feedback amplifies it. The two records move together in the cores.

review.q: What did John Tyndall measure in 1859?
choices: The age of the Earth
The speed of plate motion
Which gases absorb heat radiation
The temperature of the core
review.why: Tyndall showed that carbon dioxide, methane and water vapor absorb heat radiation while nitrogen and oxygen do not.

review.q: Lake Chicago, the early form of Lake Michigan, drained to the south. What does that tell you?
choices: The lake was smaller than today
The lake was salty
Illinois was under the ocean
Ice still blocked the northern outlets, so meltwater escaped through the Illinois River valley
review.why: With the ice sheet still to the north, the only way out was south, which is why old shorelines and outlet valleys run that way.
